canonical_topic: Selling the option instead of exercising it captures extrinsic value while shedding risk
definition: Rather than exercising an in-the-money option to lock in the risk-free intrinsic value, a holder can sell the option itself for a price between its intrinsic value and its full expected value, capturing most of the remaining extrinsic value without carrying the risk of the underlying bet.
core_idea: Selling an option can beat exercising it because a buyer will pay a premium over intrinsic value for the remaining chance of upside, letting the original holder monetize more of the option's total value while exiting the risk.
key_points: Worked example: with intrinsic value $1 million and full expected value $1.5 million, the holder might sell the ticket for $1.4 million — more than the risk-free exercise value, without keeping the risk.
The author notes a 50/50 shot at $3 million for $1.4 million is still a profitable trade for whoever buys it.
This lets the original holder capture most of the coin flip's benefit without being exposed to the risk of losing the $1 million.
relationships: Builds on the extrinsic value formula item
Foreshadows the general early-exercise rule (sell rather than exercise) discussed later in this section
trading_implications: This is the intuition behind the general market rule that options are sold rather than exercised early: selling can realize more value than exercising while eliminating downside risk.
